blind_target.authors: Sonbul, S., & Schmitt, N.
blind_target.title: Explicit and implicit lexical knowledge acquisition of collocations under different input conditions.
blind_target.evidence_quote: As a conceptual replication, Experiment 1 aimed to confirm the generalisability of Sonbul and Schmitt’s finding that repeated occurrences of low-frequency medical collocations produced declarative knowledge of these collocations and that typographic enhancement of the collocations produced more declarative knowledge than no typographic enhancement.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Typographic enhancement led to greater declarative (cued-recall) knowledge of prep+N collocations than no typographic enhancement. This result was expected since bolded collocations in Experiment 1 and Sonbul and Schmitt (2013) were learned better than unbolded collocations. What seems likely is that bolding of prep+N combinations made them more perceptually salient to the learners, drawing increased attention to the combinations and helping the learners detect formal and semantic links between the prepositions and the nouns (Boers et al., 2016; Choi, 2017; Sonbul & Schmitt, 2013). Unexpectedly, no difference was found between the amount of declarative knowledge resulting from repeated exposure to V+N collocations in the typographic enhancement and the no-typographic enhancement conditions.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Experiment 1 explicitly confirms the declarative-knowledge and enhancement findings. Experiment 2 tests their generality with non-technical collocations and explicitly reports the enhancement benefit for preposition+noun collocations but unexpectedly no benefit for verb+noun collocations. Aggregate across both experiments is mixed. The procedural-learning result in Experiment 1 is explicitly an extension, not itself a failed replication of the original null.

shipped.title_o: The efficiency of biological motion perception
shipped.outcome_quote: We replicated the previous finding of low discrimination efficiency in biological motion (Gold, Tadin, Cook, & Blake, 2008)

blind_target.authors: Gold, J., Tadin, D., Cook, S. C., & Blake, R.
blind_target.title: The efficiency of biological motion perception.
blind_target.evidence_quote: We replicated the previous finding of low discrimination efficiency in biological motion (Gold, Tadin, Cook, & Blake, 2008) and also found low detection efficiency for biological motion.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Note that the ideal thresholds for point lights and silhouette were similar, consistent with the comparable ﬁnding in a discrimination task reported by Gold et al. (2008). However, we found a slightly higher threshold for the point lights than for the silhouette whereas Gold et al. found the same threshold for the two displays. This small discrepancy was likely due to the difference in the number of frames in the walking sequence (we used 10 frames whereas Gold et al. used 20 frames).
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Low human efficiency is explicitly confirmed, but the authors also explicitly contrast ideal-observer thresholds with the original. The abstract confirms the particular low-efficiency effect rather than giving an overall verdict over all comparisons; the stated contrast requires mixed under rule 2.

items.parent_scope_question: Do not infer mixed from small magnitude variation alone. Is threshold difference a materially contrasting retested finding, or acknowledged negligible implementation variation with central efficiency result supported?

shipped.title_o: "To Share or Not to Share?" Serosorting by Hepatitis C Status in the Sharing of Drug Injection Equipment Among NHBS-IDU2 Participants
shipped.authors_o: Smith; Jewett; Burt; Zibbell; Yartel; DiNenno
shipped.outcome_quote: The survey was heavily modeled after the National HIV Behavioral Survey, which was the dataset used by the previous researchers. We found that among PWID in rural Puerto Rico, unlike in the general population, knowledge of one's own HCV status had no significant effect on the selection of one's most recent injection partner, based on his/her HCV status. We conclude that PWID in rural Puerto Rico differ from the general U.S. population when it comes to serosorting behaviors, and that these differences should be taken into account in future outreaches and intervention strategies.

blind_target.authors: Smith B.D. Jewett A. Burt R.D. Zibbell J.E. Yartel A.K. DiNenno E.
blind_target.title: “To Share or Not to Share?” serosorting by hepatitis C status in the sharing of drug injection equipment among NHBS-IDU2 participants
blind_target.evidence_quote: The current analysis replicates Model 2 from Smith et al., which examined if participants could have attempted to serosort on their last injection partner, or simply if they had knowledge of their last injection partner's HCV status ( Smith et al., 2013 ).
blind_target.outcome_quote: The findings from our data are vastly different from those found in prior work on HCV serosorting. While Smith et al. found that self-reported HCV status (either positive or negative), income, education, homelessness, and employment status were all associated with having knowledge last injection partner's HCV status in the general U.S. population, none of these served as correlates in our sample of rural Puerto Ricans. Our results did mirror the finding from the general population that age is not strongly associated with attempted serosorting, however, in that it was unrelated to having knowledge of last injection partner's HCV status.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Authors contrast the missing HCV status and other associations with Smith, while explicitly confirming age, gender and age at first injection comparisons. The broad claim of different community behavior is not an overall statement that every tested finding failed. Sample-size limitations are discussed but authors do not conclude the attempt cannot adjudicate.

blind_target.evidence_quote: In my experiment, I attempted to confirm Sonbul and Schmitt’s findings regarding declarative (explicit) knowledge by changing a number of features of their study—too many features to allow it to be defined as either an exact or an approximate replication.

blind_target.authors: Folk, C. L., & Remington, R. W.
blind_target.title: Unexpected abrupt onsets can override a top-down set for color.
blind_target.evidence_quote: In Experiment 1, rare or frequent onset cues were presented in combination with red feature targets (a red target together with one green and two white nontargets). The goal was to replicate Folk and Remington’s Experiment 3.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Experiment 1 replicated Folk and Remington’s (2015) Experiment 3 in that rare onset cues elicited validity effects, even though the target was a red feature target. Hence, the attention-driving signal elicited by rare onset cues outweighed the task-set for red color, and the cues consequently captured attention against observers’ goals. In Folk and Remington’s (2015) Experiment 3, rare onset cues elicited larger validity effects for long than short lags, suggesting that rare onset cues captured attention because of expectancy violation. In the present Experiment 1, validity effects did not depend on the trial-lag.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The main capture effect agrees, but the paper explicitly contrasts its absent lag dependence with the original; subsequent experiments also qualify claims about top-down impenetrability and color cues. Confirmation of one effect is not an overall verdict.

blind_target.authors: Cutler, A.
blind_target.title: The lexical statistics of word recognition problems caused by L2 phonetic confusion.
blind_target.evidence_quote: The current study builds on Cutler's (2005) work by examining how misperception can affect the structure of the L2 English mental lexicon. In simulating the L2 mental lexicon, a database like CELEX (Baayen et. al, 1996) is too large -it would only work for people with extremely large vocabularies. Even using the CLEARPOND (Marian et al., 2012) or KU Similarity Neighborhood calculator (Vitevitch, n.d.) for L2 learners may not be ideal, because these databases reflect the average L1 speaker's mental lexicon. Instead, we perform Cutler's three analyses using a database we built to reflect the average L2 mental lexicon: the English Vocabulary Profile Phonological database (EVP-Phon; see Methods).
blind_target.outcome_quote: The current study examined how misperception could affect the structure of the L2 English mental lexicon. Using a database built to simulate the size of the L2 English mental lexicon, we found larger counts of both pseudo-homophones and pseudo-phonological neighbors for /l/-/r/ misperception than /ɛ/-/ae/. Compared to Cutler (2005), we found fewer pseudo-homophones in terms of raw numbers, but a larger proportion of the L2 lexicon becomes homophonous for each misperception pattern.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Original finding stated in introduction: more pseudo-homophones from l/r than vowel confusion. Corresponding result agrees. Different raw totals and proportions arise in a deliberately smaller corpus; not treated as failed tests. No overall replication verdict; interpretation uncertain because authors also discuss changed counting conventions.

Further, in mice bearing orthotopic 22Rv1 human prostate tumors, we did not find a statistically significant difference in tumor weight for mice treated with DOX and iRGD compared to DOX alone, whereas the original study reported a decrease in tumor weight when DOX was coadministered with iRGD (Figure 2C; Sugahara et al., 2010). In addition, we did not find a statistically significant difference in TUNEL staining in tumor tissue between mice treated with DOX and iRGD compared to DOX alone, while the original study reported an increase in TUNEL positive staining with iRGD coadministration (Figure 2D; Sugahara et al., 2010).

blind_target.authors: de Langhe, B., van Osselaer, S. M. J., Puntoni, S., & McGill, A. L.
blind_target.title: Fooled by Heteroscedastic Randomness: Local Consistency Breeds Extremity in Price-Based Quality Inferences.
blind_target.evidence_quote: The claim selected for replication from de Langhe et al (2014) is the Study 2 claim that consumers base their predictions of quality given price on perceived covariation, in particular the presence of a price region where quality is locally consistent increases the predicted quality at high price: experiencing consistently low quality products at lower prices should lead to more extreme price-based quality predictions at higher prices.
blind_target.outcome_quote: Thus, the focal hypothesis was replicated. The test of the secondary hypothesis (H1) is given by the Price X Condition: Variance Decreasing interaction term (delta-1b). Here we found a non-significant interaction, with b = 0.03, SE = 0.08, t(513.04) = 0.37, p = 0.709, indicating that the regression slope for price in the condition where quality was consistent at high prices was not reliably different from the condition where quality was never consistent.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The original claim is explicitly described as steeper slopes for both locally consistent conditions. The focal low-price effect replicated while the tested high-price effect did not. Successful replication of the focal hypothesis is a verdict on that comparison, rather than the whole two-hypothesis attempt.

blind_target.authors: Rinaldi, L., Di Luca, S., Henik, A., & Girell, L.
blind_target.title: A helping hand putting in order: Visuomotor routines organize numerical and non-numerical sequences in space.
blind_target.evidence_quote:
The claim selected for replication from Rinaldi et al (2016; experiment 3) is that visuomotor
routines of both finger counting (FC) and reading direction (RD) influence the representation
of non-numerical ordered sequences (days of the week), so the fastest mappings result when
both routines are compatibly oriented. Reaction times were corrected for finger baseline, and
those more than two standard deviations from the overall mean were excluded from the
analysis. A 2 x 2 x 2 repeated measures ANOVA with days-direction (thumb-little finger, little
finger-thumb), hand posture (prone, supine) and language (English, Hebrew) as withinsubjects variables was carried out, yielding a significant triple interaction, such that the
compatible mappings (Mapping A for English, Mapping G for Hebrew) were the fastest.
blind_target.outcome_quote:
Thus, this replication of the claim was partially failed according to the SCORE criteria, while
the overall ANOVA and the ANOVA on English mappings did not show the effect, the
ANOVA on Hebrew mappings replicated the reported effect.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The authors explicitly judge the final combined-sample result partially failed, contrasting failed overall and English effects with replicated Hebrew effect. This final overall partial verdict supports mixed.

blind_target.authors: Saffran, J. R., Newport, E. L., & Aslin, R. N.
blind_target.title: Word segmentation: The role of distributional cues
blind_target.evidence_quote: In this paper, we describe a replication of Experiment 1 from a classic staistical word-segmentation paper by Saffran, Newport, and Aslin 1996 (henceforth: SNA96).
blind_target.outcome_quote: We were able to replicate SNA96’s finding of above-chance recognition of words in a statistical learning paradigm. However, we are not able to conclude that this learning would generalize to other stimuli – a question that SNA96 did not address. We were unable to confirm any of SNA96’s other observations.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Discussion confirms above-chance recognition but explicitly states that no other original observations were confirmed. Revised analyses use this replication’s new data, not the original data.

shipped.title_o: When Choices Are Mistakes
shipped.outcome_quote: We find robust evidence that individuals express a desire to follow canonical axioms, but perceive violations as mistakes only for a subset of them-specifically, IIA and Transitivity. In contrast, we find no evidence that violations of Independence, First-Order Stochastic Dominance, Branching, or Consistency are perceived as mistakes.

shipped.title_o: Emotional stress regulation: The role of relative frontal alpha asymmetry in shaping the stress response
shipped.authors_o: Zhang; Bachmann; Schilling; Naumann; Schächinger; Larra
shipped.outcome_quote: Although the stress induction was successful in both samples shown by increases of cortisol, heart rate, blood pressure and ratings of stress and arousal absent in the control condition, no state-dependent shift of RFA during stress induction was observed in either sample. The current study confirmed the relation between RFA at rest and cortisol, however the observed response pattern differed from the original study as RFA both pre-, and post- stress was significantly correlated to cortisol.

blind_target.authors: Zhang, X., Bachmann, P., Schilling, T. M., Naumann, E., Schächinger, H., & Larra, M. F.
blind_target.title: Emotional stress regulation: The role of relative frontal alpha asymmetry in shaping the stress response.
blind_target.evidence_quote:
The present study is foremost a direct replication of Zhang et al. (2018) to investigate the
reliability of their results.
blind_target.outcome_quote:
In conclusion, the current study could not confirm RFA as the state-dependent marker of emotional
processing as presented by Zhang et al. (2018). While RFA was again correlated to cortisol responses as
well as cardiovascular measures and subjective stress ratings indicating predictive power as a trait index,
the observed response pattern contradicted commonly accepted conceptualizations of RFA as
correlations were positive and not negative as predicted. Similarly, the previously reported state-
dependent changes in RFA could not be replicated in the current study. As such the current study
demonstrated the lack of replicability of studies supporting contemporary conceptualizations of RFA
even despite almost identical methodology.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: The conclusion gives an overall lack-of-replicability verdict for the central state-dependent RFA finding. A replicated heart-rate correlation does not outweigh that overall conclusion.

blind_target.title: Using learner corpus methods in L2 acquisition research.
blind_target.evidence_quote: The aim of the current study is to replicate Lozano and Díaz-Negrillo’s reference study using a different dataset.
blind_target.outcome_quote: The reference study did not look into NTLU of 3rd person singular -s because of its low frequency, but the misuse errors for irregular past were reported to be similar to the current study (Lozano and Díaz-Negrillo 2019, 110). While the reference study discovered a partial U-shaped developmental pattern in the oversuppliance of regular past -ed (Lozano and Díaz-Negrillo 2019, 111), the current study 44 did not show such a pattern for this or any other morpheme.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: No single overall replication verdict. The author explicitly reports both matching irregular-past error patterns and failure to recover the original U-shaped regular-past pattern. The central proficiency-order effect and article-error distribution also differ from the reference study. These are the two stated replication research questions, not incidental robustness analyses. Low frequencies limit some patterns but the author does not declare the entire attempt incapable of adjudication.
